_policy: Every pin here is refreshed at every release to the newest upstream version that has
cleared the cooldown. Adopt nothing young; adopt everything that has aged. The arithmetic
is in senbonzakura/vendoring.py and the release check is tools/check_vendor_pins.py, so
this obligation does not depend on anyone remembering it.
Hashes are recorded by the vendoring tool from what it actually downloaded, never
transcribed from a web page: a hash copied by hand or by a summarising model is a hash
nobody verified, and it would be indistinguishable from a correct one until it failed.

llama.cpp.name: llama.cpp release binaries (llama-quantize)
why: llama-quantize is the only route to a k-quant. The gguf pip package implements
quantisation for Q4_0, Q8_0 and BF16 but only DEQUANTISATION for Q4_K, Q5_K and Q6_K
(checked against gguf 0.19.0), and a Q4_K_M is a mixture of Q4_K and Q6_K. So the
k-quant algorithms exist in C++ and nowhere else we can reach.
Reimplementing them in numpy was considered and rejected: the failure mode is a model
that loads and is quietly slightly worse, which is the defect class this project has
withdrawn results over twice.
note: CPU archives only. Quantisation is CPU work, so the CUDA, Vulkan, SYCL and ROCm builds
would add hundreds of megabytes per wheel for nothing.
llama.cpp.chosen_by: tools/check_vendor_pins.py on 2026-08-17: the newest release that had cleared the 7-day cooldown. It was chosen over b10250, which a human had picked by eye, and over b10456, which was hours old.

llama_conversion.name: llama.cpp conversion package (convert_hf_to_gguf.py + conversion/)
why: Not in the gguf pip package: its scripts/ holds only the dump, hash, endian, metadata and
editor tools. And convert_hf_to_gguf.py alone is NOT enough. As of b10355 it is a 307-line
entry point that does `from conversion import ...`; the real work is 85 modules and 845 KB
in conversion/. Fetching the one file gives a stub that fails at import, which is exactly
what the first attempt at this produced.
Fetched at build time from the source archive at the pinned tag and hash-verified, NOT
committed. An 859 KB, 87-file third-party package in our tree would make every pin bump an
87-file diff, and 'reviewable in a diff' stops being true at that size. Committing it would
buy the appearance of reviewability rather than the fact of it.
The module count and size here were MEASURED on 2026-08-18 from the extracted package. The
figures they replace, 158 modules and 752 KB, were written a day earlier alongside the
unmeasured hash described below, by the same commit and for the same reason: nothing had
been downloaded yet. Three claims, one fetch that never happened.
Its cost is that architecture support freezes at the pinned tag, which is why the
refresh-every-release rule matters here as much as for the binaries: a new architecture
landing upstream reaches us at the next release rather than never.

gguf_py_note: gguf-py/gguf/ is kept because the converter's first real statement is `import gguf`,
and the PyPI package of that name IS NOT THE SAME CODE. Measured on 2026-08-18: PyPI
gguf 0.19.0 and this tag's gguf-py both declare version 0.19.0, and the PyPI one has
no MODEL_ARCH.LFM2_MOE and no GEMMA4_ASSISTANT. The result was that conversion/lfm2.py
failed to import, while --print-supported-models still advertised Lfm2MoeForCausalLM,
because that list is built from a static registry rather than from what imported.
A claim of support the machinery could not deliver, presenting as green.
No version constraint can express this: the two share a version NUMBER and differ in
contents, so a floor, a ceiling and a pin are all equally unable to tell them apart.
Vendoring gguf-py from the same tag makes the converter and its library consistent by
construction, which is the only check that holds.
any.licence_note: LICENSE is kept from the same archive so the MIT notice we redistribute is the verbatim text at the pinned tag, not a copy of MIT typed from memory. MIT requires the copyright notice travel with the work; a paraphrase does not discharge that.

_hash_note: The value that sat here until 2026-08-18 was NEVER MEASURED. It was written on 2026-08-17
in the same commit whose own message says 'the conversion package is consequently NOT yet
fetched', because codeload was throttling; so it recorded a hash for an archive nobody had
downloaded. That is precisely what the policy above forbids, and it went in three lines
under the line forbidding it. It was caught on the first real fetch, by the check refusing
to extract. Removed rather than corrected in place, so the next fetch records it the only
legitimate way: from bytes that actually arrived.
Two hashes are kept from now on, because this URL is not the same kind of object as a
release asset. `any` is the source ARCHIVE, which the forge generates on request, so its
bytes can change with the compression in use on the day while every file inside stays
identical; a mismatch there warns. `content` is a hash over the EXTRACTED files, sorted,
